s1.quote: The wreck lies on its starboard side, with the port railing uppermost at about 23m. … The depth here is about 32m. … Not for novices, but you can have a good dive without getting into decompression.

s2.quote: DEPTH: 29m … SIZE OF WRECK: 126m long … The Kyarra usually has permanent buoys tied to it, which surface on slack water.

s3.quote: lies one mile (1.6 km) off Anvil Point … remains popular with divers

mooring.value: Permanent buoys usually tied to the wreck, surfacing at slack water

highlights.text: 126 m liner on its starboard side

hazards.text: Debris-filled interior; swim-throughs no longer safe

summary.text: A large steamship lying on her starboard side about a mile off Anvil Point near Swanage, with the upper rail near 23 m and the seabed around 30 m. Long enough to need a full dive to tour, best done at slack water.

sites.name: MV Aeolian Sky

s1.quote: but it sank by the bow in 29m of water, 12 miles from the Bill of Portland … has now been cleared by explosives to 18m … It lies on the port side with the decks facing east and the bows to the south.

s2.quote: a large bow bulge rests against the seabed at 30m … rising as shallow as 20m. … Shallow enough for less-experienced divers to make worthwhile no-stop dives

s3.quote: Approx. depth 30 metres … The ship was lying on her port side

highlights.text: Open hatches, companionways and large windows

hazards.text: Current picks up rapidly after slack water
Divers on delayed SMBs can drift widely

summary.text: A modern cargo ship lying on her port side in about 30 m south of St Aldhelm's Head, with the deck as shallow as roughly 18 to 20 m. Easy penetration and a recognisable layout make it popular, but it must be dived at slack water.

sites.depthNote: Upper deck about 18-20 m, seabed about 30 m

sites.name: SS Binnendijk

s1.quote: Least echo sounder depth 17.3 in general depth 25.6M. … Main wreckage dimensions about 120 x 30m, orientated 070/250 deg.

s2.quote: Binnendijk's wreck is on Lulworth Banks at a depth of 75 to 89 feet (23 to 27 m). … The site is relatively sheltered by Portland Bill, but is near Portland Race, so can be subject to strong currents.

summary.text: A large cargo steamer mined in 1939 and now a broken-up wreck on Lulworth Banks, nicknamed 'The Benny'. It lies roughly 17 to 27 m down, spread over an area about 120 by 30 m.

sites.depthNote: Least depth 17.3 m, general depth 25.6 m

s1.quote: Wreck lies in 38m depth, intact, standing 5m above the seabed. … Upright in general depth of 38m, the top of the conning tower being at 32m;

s2.publisher: Dorset Council Historic Environment Record (Historic England designation)
s2.quote: the site lies in approximately 30-40m of water, east of Portland, Dorset. … While the sea bed drops to 38-39m, the depth to the conning tower is 32m.

access.value: Designated protected wreck (Protection of Wrecks Act 1973); 50 m protected area

summary.text: An intact early Royal Navy submarine sitting upright on the seabed in about 38 m, with the conning tower top at 32 m. It is a designated protected wreck managed by Historic England, east of Portland.

s1.quote: She lay in 90 - 105 ft, with her stern in the sand and bow raised above the seabed. … HMSM M2 has been cited as a designated vessel under the Protection of Military Remains Act 1986. … it is an offence to enter or damage the hull structure.

s2.quote: sits upright on a relatively flat seabed at a maximum depth of 31m around the bow and 35m at the stern. … Salvage divers discovered that the hangar doors were wide open.

s3.quote: about 100 ft (30 m) below the surface at low tide … She is a popular dive for scuba divers.

access.value: Protected place under Protection of Military Remains Act 1986 (war grave): do not enter or damage the hull

highlights.text: Submarine with seaplane hangar and distinctive conning tower

hazards.text: War grave: entering the hull is an offence
Silts up quickly; visibility can be poor

summary.text: A large WWI monitor-class submarine carrying a seaplane hangar, lying largely intact and upright in 30 to 35 m off Chesil Beach. She is a war grave protected under military remains law, so look but do not touch or enter.

s1.quote: Portland Port Ltd. has banned all diving on the HOOD from 1st January 2004 for an indefinite period. … has degraded and is now collapsing in on itself.

notDiveSite.reason: Blockship upside down and collapsing; Portland Port banned all diving on it from 2004

s1.quote: The wreck lies on a sandy bed at a depth of 30 metres (98 ft). … Ship sunk in 1917 near Portland Bill, now a dive site.

s2.quote: Approx. depth 30 metres … Sunk by a German Submarine, 10.5 miles SW of Lyme Regis.

summary.text: A Danish steamer torpedoed by a U-boat in 1917 and now resting on sand at about 30 m in Lyme Bay, roughly 10 miles south-west of Lyme Regis. A boat-only wreck dive.

s1.quote: Approx. depth 33 metres … Position 50 36.13N 02 58.73W

s2.quote: French ship sunk in Lyme Bay in 1917. Now a dive site.

summary.text: A French collier torpedoed by UB-40 in 1917 and now a wreck dive in Lyme Bay, lying in roughly 33 m.

s1.quote: She lies in the middle of Lyme Bay in 138 feet of water on a sandy bottom. … The wreck was salvaged by Mayer & Newman who removed much of her armour plating and the bronze propellers.

s2.quote: After several hits she turned turtle and sank.

summary.text: A pre-dreadnought battleship sunk as a gunnery target in 1913; she lies capsized on sand in the middle of Lyme Bay at around 42 m, partly stripped by salvors.

s1.quote: Standing upright in 44 metres, with her deck at 38 metres she is still an awesome sight. … She is totally intact, showing little deterioration. … being scuttled in 40 M of water.

summary.text: An American S-class submarine lent to the Royal Navy and scuttled off Portland in 1947 as an asdic target. She sits upright and largely intact, with the deck at about 38 m and the seabed near 44 m.

s1.quote: The wreck of the LST now lies at a depth of 50 metres (160 ft). … classed as protected wrecks, and so diving without a licence is not possible.

s2.quote: that lie 50m deep off the Devon coast … Scheduling means that divers can still dive the sites without a licence

access.value: Exercise Tiger war grave; scheduled monument (Historic England says dive without licence but respect the site)

summary.text: A US Navy tank landing ship torpedoed by E-boats during the 1944 Exercise Tiger rehearsal and now a war grave about 50 m down in Lyme Bay. A technical-depth dive on a protected site.

s1.quote: 34 m (112 ft) below sea level on a gravel seabed … The machinery is right aft and the bridge is right forward while everything in the middle was cargo space.

s2.quote: Canadian steamer ALBERT C FIELD, 1764 tons, bombed by aircraft in June 1944. Depth 40 metres.

s3.quote: The highest parts of the Wreck are the boilers. … No-one seems to have dived this wreck … This is one to keep well clear of.

hazards.text: Ammunition cargo; advised to keep well clear

summary.text: A Canadian steamer bombed in June 1944 while carrying ammunition; the wreck is badly broken, with boilers the highest point, in roughly 34 to 40 m south of Anvil Point. The Dorset record warns divers to stay clear of the explosive cargo.

s1.quote: lies on its port side on white sand at a depth of about 40 m (130 ft) … Her stern is broken up but her bow, boilers, engine and helm can all be identified.

s2.quote: Dutch steamer AJAX, 942 tons, bombed by aircraft in August 1940. Depth 40 metres.

summary.text: A Dutch steamer bombed in 1940, lying on her port side on white sand at about 40 m off the Isle of Wight. The stern is broken up but the bow, boilers and engine are recognisable.

s1.quote: British steamer MENDI, 4230 tons, sank following collision in February 1917. Depth 40 metres.

s2.quote: designated Mendi's wreck site as a protected war grave

access.value: Protected war grave (Protection of Military Remains Act); no removing artefacts

summary.text: The troopship Mendi sank in a 1917 collision south of the Isle of Wight with heavy loss of South African lives. She lies in about 40 m, is now a protected war grave and is badly collapsed apart from the bow and stern.

sites.name: HMT Warwick Deeping

s1.quote: lying along the tide in 34m … the wreck is upright and pretty much intact … Slack water is essential and occurs 10 minutes after high water or 45 minutes before low water Dover.

s2.quote: lies in 37 meters of water to the south of the Isle of Wight … completely upright and largely intact on a gravel seabed

s4.quote: lies in 35 metres (115 ft) of water … a popular wreck diving site

highlights.text: Intact trawler with 4.7in gun at the bow
Iron four-blade propeller exposed by scour

hazards.text: Strong tide; slack water short and essential
Net draped over the forward wreck; scour under stern

summary.text: A small armed trawler lost in 1940, sitting upright and largely intact on gravel in 34 to 37 m south of the Isle of Wight. It lies along the tide, so a short slack-water window and careful shotting matter.

sites.depthNote: Deckhouse roof about 30 m, seabed 34-37 m

s1.quote: in 30 metres (98 feet) of water

s2.quote: This boat is a dive site … Depth: 110 feet (34 meters) … The wreck of U-1195 was located in position 50.33.17N, 00.56.09W.

summary.text: A German Type VIIC U-boat sunk by depth charges in April 1945 and now a dive site in roughly 30 to 34 m south-east of the Isle of Wight.

s1.quote: The wreck is designated as a controlled site under the Protection of Military Remains Act 1986 … all diving on her is strictly prohibited.

notDiveSite.reason: Designated controlled site under Protection of Military Remains Act 1986; diving prohibited

sites.name: Royal Adelaide (1865 ship)

s1.quote: Fore-deck winch, chain locker and other wreckage remain about 120 off-shore in about 12m of water. … The part that remains of the hull today is being rapidly eroded.

summary.text: The 1872 wreck of a sailing ship on Chesil Beach; only scattered winch, chain locker and hull remains survive in about 12 m of water just offshore, and the hull is eroding fast.

sites.depthNote: Remains of wreckage about 12 m (1984 record)

s1.quote: About 400m out, the seabed levels off at a depth of 18m and becomes mainly sand and fine gravel. … On average 1-5m, depending on tides and wave action. … Be prepared for waves and undertow during entries and exits

s2.quote: one of the best known shore dives in the UK. … The cove is a reasonably shallow shore dive.

hazards.text: Waves and undertow on entry and exit

summary.text: One of Britain's best-known shore dives, entered from Chesil's pebble beach at Portland and descending past ledges to a sand-and-gravel seabed near 18 m. Visibility is typically 1 to 5 m but can reach 10 m in calm spells; surf and undertow make entries tricky.

s1.quote: lies flat against the seabed at 35m. … Suitable for sports divers making no-stop dives … The wreck lies partly across the tide, with the bow just to the west of north.

s2.quote: The site was designated under the Protection of Wrecks Act on 17 August 2016.

access.value: Designated protected wreck (Protection of Wrecks Act 1973); managed by Historic England

summary.text: A WWI naval trawler mined in 1917 and now a protected wreck south of St Alban's Head, lying partly across the tide with the rudder on the seabed near 35 m. Small enough for a no-stop dive yet complex enough to reward more time.
